targetedChanges.name: Hominini: humans and chimpanzees
targetedChanges.short_desc: A taxonomic tribe that includes humans and chimpanzees. “Hominin” is also often used for members of the human lineage after the split from Pan.
targetedChanges.date_note: Taxonomic definitions differ. The imported 9–8 million BCE interval conflated a taxon with an evolutionary divergence; no single founding date is assigned.

targetedChanges.name: Origins of the human lineage
targetedChanges.short_desc: The earliest members of the human lineage are identified from fragmentary fossil evidence and competing phylogenetic interpretations.
targetedChanges.date_note: A distinct, exactly dated “emergence of Hominini” at 7 million BCE is not established. See Sahelanthropus (31), Graecopithecus (29), and the Pan–Homo divergence (32). The original row is retained.

targetedChanges.name: Graecopithecus freybergi
targetedChanges.short_desc: Late Miocene ape remains from Greece and Bulgaria, proposed as possible early members of the human lineage on dental evidence.
targetedChanges.date_note: Approximately 7.2 million years old. The proposed hominin affinity is disputed; this does not establish a European origin of humans.

targetedChanges.short_desc: Sahelanthropus, from Chad around 7 million years ago, is a candidate early hominin. Cranial and limb evidence has been interpreted as supporting bipedalism.
targetedChanges.date_note: Around 7 million years ago; rounded deep-time placement. Bipedalism and phylogenetic placement have been debated, including new limb analyses published in 2026.

targetedChanges.short_desc: The human and chimpanzee lineages separated through an evolutionary process whose timing depends on fossil interpretation and molecular models.
targetedChanges.date_note: A broad approximately 8–6 million-year divergence window, not a dated individual ancestor or a two-million-year lifespan.

targetedChanges.short_desc: Stone artefacts at Lomekwi 3 in Kenya were reported from deposits around 3.3 million years old, predating the known fossil record of Homo.
targetedChanges.date_note: Age of an archaeological assemblage, not proof of the first stone use anywhere; the toolmakers are not securely identified.

targetedChanges.name: Early Homo at Ledi-Geraru
targetedChanges.short_desc: The LD 350-1 mandible from Ethiopia documents early Homo around 2.80–2.75 million years ago.
targetedChanges.date_note: Fossil age bounds, not the duration of the genus. Approximate BCE conversion from geological ages, rounded to millennia; additional Ledi-Geraru finds were reported in 2025.

targetedChanges.name: Early fire-use claims
targetedChanges.short_desc: Some early African sites have been proposed as evidence for hominin fire use, but natural burning and archaeological context complicate interpretation.
targetedChanges.date_note: The imported 2.0–1.7 million-year window represents disputed early claims, not established controlled fire. Stronger in-cave evidence is recorded separately at Wonderwerk (41).

targetedChanges.name: Fire at Wonderwerk Cave
targetedChanges.short_desc: Burned bone and plant ash inside Wonderwerk Cave provide evidence of fire in an Early Acheulean archaeological context around one million years ago.
targetedChanges.date_note: Approximate BCE placement of a 1.0-million-year-old context. This does not prove that hominins could ignite fire, or securely identify the fire users as Homo erectus.

targetedChanges.name: Early Homo sapiens at Jebel Irhoud
targetedChanges.short_desc: Moroccan fossils combine a modern-looking face with a more archaic braincase and document an early stage in the Homo sapiens lineage.
targetedChanges.date_note: Thermoluminescence age 315 ± 34 thousand years. BCE bounds are approximate, rounded to millennia; this is an age estimate, not a species lifespan or a single moment of origin.

targetedChanges.name: Apidima 1: proposed early Homo sapiens in Europe
targetedChanges.short_desc: A partial Greek cranium was interpreted in 2019 as Homo sapiens older than 210,000 years, suggesting an early Eurasian dispersal.
targetedChanges.date_note: A minimum age and a debated taxonomic interpretation. The rounded timeline placement is not proof of a precisely dated migration or its failure.

targetedChanges.name: Late Homo erectus at Ngandong
targetedChanges.short_desc: The Ngandong bone bed in Java records a late known occurrence of Homo erectus, modelled at 117,000–108,000 years ago.
targetedChanges.date_note: Approximate BCE bounds rounded to millennia. A last known fossil occurrence does not establish the actual extinction date.

targetedChanges.name: Clothing inferred from lice evolution
targetedChanges.short_desc: Genetic modelling of clothing lice suggests that clothing was in use at least 83,000 years ago and possibly as early as 170,000 years ago.
targetedChanges.date_note: Indirect, model-dependent inference rather than surviving clothing. Approximate BCE bounds rounded to millennia.

targetedChanges.short_desc: The Youngest Toba Tuff eruption occurred around 74,000 years ago in Sumatra. Its proposed role in a severe human population bottleneck remains debated.
targetedChanges.date_note: The eruption is well attested; the original assertion that humanity was reduced to 3,000–10,000 individuals is not treated as established fact.

targetedChanges.name: Early cave marks at Maltravieso
targetedChanges.short_desc: Uranium-series dating of carbonate over a hand stencil was interpreted as indicating art older than 64,800 years and possible Neanderthal authorship.
targetedChanges.date_note: A minimum-age claim, with debates over carbonate–pigment relationships and authorship. Approximate BCE placement; this is not an exact painting date.

targetedChanges.name: Early occupation at Madjedbebe
targetedChanges.short_desc: Excavations at Madjedbebe in northern Australia were interpreted as evidence of human occupation around 65,000 years ago.
targetedChanges.date_note: Approximate BCE placement rounded to millennia. This is a site-based age estimate; the earliest peopling of Sahul and the interpretation of older deposits remain debated.

targetedChanges.name: Narrative cave art in Sulawesi
targetedChanges.short_desc: A scene at Leang Karampuang showing human-like figures with a pig was dated to a minimum age of 51,200 years.
targetedChanges.date_note: Minimum age, not an exact painting date. Approximately 49,200 BCE. A 2026 study reports a still older Sulawesi hand stencil of at least 67,800 years (not a narrative scene): https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09968-y

targetedChanges.name: Late Neanderthal disappearance in Europe
targetedChanges.short_desc: Improved radiocarbon models place the end of the European Mousterian around 41,030–39,260 calibrated years BP, with regional variation.
targetedChanges.date_note: The 2014 model gives 95.4% bounds for archaeological disappearance. BP uses the fixed 1950 reference, unlike the viewer-relative “years ago” tooltip. Rounded BCE conversion; not a globally synchronous extinction.

targetedChanges.name: Late Denisovan evidence at Baishiya
targetedChanges.short_desc: A Denisovan rib from Baishiya Karst Cave was identified in a layer dated approximately 48,000–32,000 years ago.
targetedChanges.date_note: Approximate BCE conversion rounded to millennia. This dates fossil-bearing sediment, not Denisovan extinction; the imported 28,000–13,000 BCE extinction claim was unsupported.

targetedChanges.name: Neanderthal cord at Abri du Maras
targetedChanges.short_desc: A three-ply cord fragment attached to a stone tool provides direct evidence of Neanderthal fibre technology.
targetedChanges.date_note: Context dated about 52,000–41,000 years ago, placed approximately in BCE. Older than the imported 28,000-year rope claim; an archaeological occurrence does not date the invention of cordage.

targetedChanges.name: Human footprints at White Sands
